title: Forklift traffic routes and pedestrian segregation
audience: Cleaners working in warehouses where forklifts and pedestrians share space.
learningOutcomes: Identify forklift traffic routes and pedestrian walkways on the site plan.
Keep clear of forklift routes, and use segregated walkways only.
Stop and withdraw when a forklift route crosses the cleaning area.

instruction.heading: Why routes and walkways are separated
instruction.body: Forklifts move on set routes, and pedestrians should use walkways that are kept apart from those routes. The reason is that a forklift driver has a limited view, a load can block the view ahead, and a forklift turning at speed covers more space than the driver can always see. A cleaner who works close to a route is exposed to a strike, to being crushed against racking or a wall, or to being hit by a load that has been lifted or lowered. The Safe Work Australia guidance on warehouse traffic management states that the best approach is to keep pedestrians and forklifts apart, and that where that is not possible, the layout should be changed to reduce the time people spend in forklift areas. The same guidance says that access to forklift areas should be limited to operators and supervisors. Mark both the routes and the walkways on the site plan before you start, so that you know which area is which before you are in it.

instruction.heading: Keeping clear of blind spots and turning areas
instruction.body: Keep clear of forklift routes and of blind spots. A blind spot is any place a driver cannot see from the cab, such as the area behind a stacked load, the corner of an aisle where racking meets a cross-aisle, the space beside a forklift when it turns, and the gap at a dock door as a trailer is backed in. The guidance uses the term blind spots, and it recommends safety railings or bollards to stop pedestrians stepping into traffic from those points, and mirrors, cameras, sensors or alarms so that drivers can see around vehicles. Do not step into a route to reach a corner, and do not work in a route while a forklift is moving. A forklift that has stopped is not safe to work next to, because it can start again without warning. Where a route crosses the cleaning area, withdraw to a safe location that is not in a blind spot, and ask the site controller for a revised pedestrian route before you go back.

instruction.heading: Segregation, barriers and the stop-work right
instruction.body: Use barriers, signs and the site's segregation where they are provided. The guidance suggests high-impact barriers, containment fences and enforced exclusion zones where people and plant must be close, and it notes that a load should not block a driver's view. Report a missing barrier, a blocked walkway or a near miss at once, and record the location and time. Do not move a barrier to shorten a route, and do not climb over one. Under the Commonwealth Work Health and Safety Act, a worker may cease, or refuse to carry out, work where they have a reasonable concern that doing the work would expose them to a serious risk to their health or safety from an immediate or imminent exposure to a hazard. That right may be relevant to a cleaner who sees a forklift route cross the area without warning. Other state and territory laws may apply to the site, so check the law that applies where the site is located. Record the stop on the job file, with the reason and the site's response.

instruction.heading: Forklifts, licences and what this lesson does not authorise
instruction.body: Operating a forklift is a licensed activity. The SafeWork NSW guidance states that a worker needs a high risk work licence with the relevant class to operate a forklift in NSW, and it describes the forklift truck class (LF) as covering a forklift with a mast and an elevating load carriage with fork arms or another attachment, and the order picking class (LO) for order-picking trucks. The SafeWork SA class list shows the forklift truck class LF and the order picking forklift class LO. The SafeWork NSW page does not say whether a licence is needed to direct or supervise a forklift, and this lesson does not decide that question. This lesson does not teach or authorise you to operate, move or direct a forklift, and completing it does not grant any licence or plant authority.

instruction.heading: Worked boundary: a route, a corner and a stacked load
instruction.body: A cleaning corridor runs parallel to a forklift route for part of its length, and at one end it meets a cross-aisle where a stacked load of cartons blocks the view. A barrier is in place along the route side, but it has a gap where a cart has been pushed through. The cleaner's task is to clean the floor of the corridor. Under this lesson, the part of the corridor beside the route is kept clear, and the cleaner works only on the far side of the barrier. The corner at the cross-aisle is a blind spot, so the cleaner does not clean it, and does not stand near it while a forklift is in the area. The gap in the barrier is reported at once, and the cleaner does not move the cart, which belongs to the site. The cleaner records the gap, the stacked load, the time, and the person told, and asks the site controller for a revised pedestrian route for the corridor. If a forklift route moves across the corridor while the cleaner is in it, the cleaner withdraws to a safe location, and does not return until the site confirms the route is clear of the area.

procedure: Mark forklift routes, pedestrian walkways, blind spots and crossing points on the site plan before you start.
Keep clear of forklift routes and blind spots, and do not step into a route to reach a corner.
Work only on the pedestrian side of any barrier, and use segregated walkways where they are provided.
Withdraw to a safe location, and ask the site controller for a revised pedestrian route when a route crosses the cleaning area.
Do not move barriers, carts or loads to shorten a route, and do not climb over a barrier.
Report missing barriers, blocked walkways, blind spots and near misses at once, and record the location and time.
Cease work and withdraw if you have a reasonable concern about a serious risk from an immediate or imminent hazard, and record the stop.

workedExamples.situation: A forklift route now crosses the corridor assigned for cleaning, and the walkway has been moved to the far side of a stacked load.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and what is recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: Withdraw to the safe location, which is outside any blind spot, and do not work around the moving plant. Do not return until the site controller has given a revised pedestrian route that keeps you out of the route. Record the change, the stacked load, the time and the person you spoke to. The corridor is cleaned only in the part the site confirms as walkway.

workedExamples.situation: A barrier between a forklift route and a walkway has a gap, and a cleaner notices that a cart has been pushed through it to reach the other side.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you move the cart, and what do you report?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not move the cart or close the gap. Keep to the walkway side, and report the gap and the cart at once to the site controller, with the location and time. Record the report, and ask for the gap to be fixed before the walkway is used for cleaning. The cleaner does not work in the gap, and does not use the walkway until the site has confirmed it is safe.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is asked by a forklift operator to step back from a stacked load so the operator can reverse past it, and the cleaner is standing in the operator's blind spot.
workedExamples.reasoning: Move out of the route and out of the blind spot to a position the operator can see, or to a safe location. Do not wait to be told twice, and do not stand behind the load to finish a task. Report the near miss to the site controller, with the location and time, and record it. The cleaner does not return to the area until the site confirms the route and the walkway.

equipmentAndPpe: Site plan showing forklift routes, pedestrian walkways, blind spots and crossing points.
High-visibility clothing and safety footwear as the site requires.
Radio or call point, where the site provides one for contacting the site controller.
Barriers, signs and exclusion markings provided by the site. The cleaner does not install, move or remove them.

Personal protective equipment is used after the layout and segregation controls have been checked. Safe Work Australia describes personal protective equipment as among the least effective controls, to be used after higher-level controls such as segregation.

commonErrors.error: Working behind a stacked load in a forklift aisle, where the driver cannot see.
commonErrors.prevention: Stay out of routes and blind spots. Ask the site controller for a revised route instead.

commonErrors.error: Moving a barrier or a cart to reach a corner.
commonErrors.prevention: Never move a barrier. Report it and ask for a revised route.

commonErrors.error: Ignoring a near miss because nothing happened.
commonErrors.prevention: Report the near miss at once, and record its location, time and what happened.

commonErrors.error: Stepping into a route to finish a corner while a forklift is stopped nearby.
commonErrors.prevention: A stopped forklift can start without warning. Stay out of the route until the site confirms it is clear.

commonErrors.error: Continuing to clean after a forklift route has moved into the area.
commonErrors.prevention: Withdraw to a safe location, and return only when the site has confirmed the route.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Safe Work Australia's guidance on warehouse traffic management says that the best approach is to keep pedestrians and forklifts apart, and that access to forklift areas should be limited to operators and supervisors. The guidance describes exclusion zones, high-impact barriers and blind spot controls as options to consider. The site's own traffic management plan governs the controls at a particular site.

Under section 84 of the Commonwealth Work Health and Safety Act 2011, as in the July 2024 compilation checked for this lesson, a worker may cease or refuse work where they have a reasonable concern that doing it would expose them to a serious risk to their health or safety from an immediate or imminent exposure to a hazard.

Operating a forklift is a licensed activity. The SafeWork NSW guidance says a high risk work licence with the relevant class is needed to operate a forklift in NSW, and the SafeWork SA class list includes the forklift truck class LF.

This lesson does not grant any licence, plant-safety approval, certificate or specialist authority, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist. It does not authorise operating, moving or directing a forklift.

qualityStandard: Forklift routes, walkways, blind spots and crossing points marked on the simulated plan.
Withdrawal demonstrated when a route crosses the cleaning area in the role-play, with a revised pedestrian route requested.
Missing barrier and near miss reported at once, with location and time, in the simulation.
No barrier, cart or load moved by the cleaner, and no work in an active route or a blind spot.
documentationEvidence: Annotated site plan showing routes, walkways, blind spots and crossing points.
Near-miss, barrier and route-change record, with location, time and person told.
Record of any stop-work decision, with the reason and the site's response.
Written revised pedestrian route from the site controller, before work resumes in the affected area.
summary: Mark routes, walkways and blind spots on the plan before you start.
Keep clear of routes and blind spots, and work only on the pedestrian side of any barrier.
Withdraw and request a revised route when a route crosses the area; do not move barriers.
Report barriers, blocked walkways and near misses at once, and use the stop-work right when a serious risk is immediate.

knowledgeChecks.question: A forklift route crosses your cleaning area. What is correct?
options: Withdraw to a safe location and request a revised pedestrian route
Work around it quickly while the forklift is turning and the path is open
Move the barrier so the route is clear for you and your equipment

knowledgeChecks.question: Why are blind spots a risk for pedestrians near forklifts?
options: They are usually dark and hard to see in the aisle
A driver may not be able to see a person there
They are usually slippery, so the driver slows down
They are where the walkway ends and the racks start

knowledgeChecks.question: A barrier is in your way. What do you do?
options: Move it, since it is only a barrier in the way
Step over it, since it is a low barrier and quick to pass
Do not move it; report it and ask for a revised route

knowledgeChecks.question: You have a reasonable concern that the work would expose you to an immediate serious risk from a forklift. What is correct?
options: Keep working and report it at the end of the shift, once the job is done
Cease the work and withdraw to a safe location, then record and report it
Ask a colleague to take the risk for you, since they are already close to the route
